# The Tension or Compression Bar {#sec-zugstab}

## Stress {#sec-spannung}

As an example of a tension bar we consider a tow bar as shown in @fig-abschleppstange.
In the mechanical model this bar is treated as a *bar* with length $l$ and cross-sectional area $A$.
The bar axis is the line connecting the centroids of the cross-sections.

![Tow bar as an example of a tension bar](images/Abschleppstange.svg){#fig-abschleppstange}

At both ends a force $F$ acts in the direction of the bar.
These forces are exerted on the bar by the two cars in the directions indicated in @fig-abschleppstange.
A precise specification of the support conditions is not required for the following considerations.

Using the method of sections, the internal forces in the bar can be determined.
Since only a load in the direction of the bar is applied, there is only a normal force, and this follows from the equilibrium condition in the horizontal direction as

$$
\sum H=0 \rightarrow N=F \; .
$$ {#eq-gg-N}

It is constant over the length of the bar and has a positive sign, i.e. a tensile force acts in the bar.

In the next step we introduce the important concept of *stress*.
To do so we cut the bar *normal* to the bar axis and consider the forces acting on the cut surfaces, see @fig-normalspannungen.
If the normal force $N$ is distributed uniformly over the cut area $A$, we obtain the following quantity

$$
\sigma = \dfrac{N}{A} = \dfrac{F}{A} \; ,
$$ {#eq-spannung}

which we call stress.
As can be seen from @fig-normalspannungen, $\sigma$ represents internal forces distributed over an area whose resultant is exactly equal to the normal force $N$.
Typical units for stress are, for example, N/mm² or Pa = N/m².

![Normal stresses in the cross-section](images/Normalspannungen.svg){#fig-normalspannungen}

Furthermore, @fig-normalspannungen shows that $\sigma$ acts normal to the cut surface.
This stress is therefore called *normal stress*.
In addition, a further classification is made according to sign: a negative normal stress is called *compressive stress*, a positive one *tensile stress*.
According to [Newton]{.smallcaps}'s third law, a stress of equal magnitude but in the *opposite* direction acts on the opposite cut surface, see @fig-normalspannungen.
Each of the two parts must be in equilibrium!

In the next step we no longer make the cut $s-s$ normal to the bar axis, but inclined by the angle $\alpha$ relative to the vertical, see @fig-schraeger-schnitt.

![Stress on an inclined cut surface](images/schraegerSchnitt.svg){#fig-schraeger-schnitt}

The stress, which is now no longer a normal stress, on the cut surface $A'$ is equal to

$$
\sigma' = \dfrac{F}{A'} = \dfrac{F}{A}\cos\alpha \; .
$$ {#eq-spannung-schraeg}

Using trigonometric functions, this stress is split into a component normal and tangential to the cut surface:

$$
\sigma = \sigma'\cos\alpha = \dfrac{F}{A}\cos^2\alpha
\quad \text{and} \quad
\tau = \sigma'\sin\alpha = \dfrac{F}{A}\sin\alpha\cos\alpha \; .
$$ {#eq-sigma-tau}

$\sigma$ is then again a normal stress, and the stress $\tau$ acting in the cut surface we shall call *shear stress*.
Consequently, stresses can also be classified according to their direction of action relative to the cut surface into normal and shear stresses.

![Normal and shear stresses](images/Schubspannungen.svg){#fig-schubspannungen}

From relation ([-@eq-sigma-tau]) it becomes clearly apparent that stresses depend on the *orientation* of the cut surface to which they are referred.
In the present case $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are a function of the angle $\alpha$.

## Strain {#sec-dehnung}

Next we want to investigate what happens to the tow bar in @fig-abschleppstange when the load is applied.
Even if it is hard to see with the naked eye, the tow bar will stretch due to the tensile force, i.e. it elongates slightly.
In @fig-gleichmassdehnung the bar is shown before and after load application.
The change in total length is $\Delta l$.
In addition, we also want to know the longitudinal displacement of a cross-section at an arbitrary position $x$.
This is measured by the function $u$ (@fig-gleichmassdehnung).

![Deformation of the tension bar under constant normal force](images/Gleichmassdehnung.svg){#fig-gleichmassdehnung}

The distribution of $u$ for a *constant* normal force is also shown there.
Starting from zero at the left end, it increases linearly and reaches the value $\Delta l$ at the right end.
Another important quantity, namely the *strain*, is obtained when the change in length $\Delta l$ is referred to the original length $l$:

$$
\ve = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} \; .
$$ {#eq-dehnung}

This value equals the slope of the longitudinal displacement $u$.
The strain can also be understood as the relative change in distance between two neighbouring points.

Unlike in @fig-gleichmassdehnung, the change in length is usually barely perceptible to the naked eye, i.e. $\Delta l \ll l$.
Consequently, the strain is also very small ($\ve\ll 1$) and for this reason is usually given in percent or per mille.
A positive strain corresponds to an elongation of the bar, negative values to a shortening of the bar.
In that case one often also speaks of compression.

If, for example, a variable distributed load acts along the bar, so that the normal force is also variable, then the displacement is no longer a linear function, see @fig-veraenderliche-dehnung.

![Deformation of the tension bar under variable normal force](images/veraenderlicheDehnung.svg){#fig-veraenderliche-dehnung}

The strain can still be interpreted as the slope of $u$ at position $x$.
Using the first derivative we obtain the slope, i.e. the strain:

$$
\myBox{\ve(x)=\dfrac{du}{dx}} \; .
$$ {#eq-dehnung-dudx}

In contrast to the first load case, this is now no longer constant over the length of the bar.
If the strain is known, the displacement and hence the change in length of the bar can be determined by integrating the above relation.

## Constitutive Law {#sec-werkstoffgesetz}

We have now introduced two important new mechanical quantities: stress and strain.
But is there also a relationship between the two?
To this end we carry out a tensile test, see @fig-zugversuch.
A tensile specimen, usually of circular cross-section, is mounted in a suitable machine.
The lower edge of the specimen is supported such that it cannot move.
In contrast, the upper edge can be moved by a hydraulic cylinder.
This results in the mechanical model shown in @fig-zugversuch.
It is the same system as the tow bar.
Both the force $F$ and the displacement $\Delta l$ at the upper edge are measured and recorded during the test.

![Tensile test](images/Zugversuch.svg){#fig-zugversuch}

::: {.callout-important .video-box icon=false}
## Video

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fEbkcTBNiGg >}}
:::

If, from the measured data, one computes the stress according to ([-@eq-spannung]) and the strain according to ([-@eq-dehnung]) and plots them in a diagram, one obtains the curve shown in @fig-arbeitsdiagramm.
The specimen in this case is a mild steel.
The relationship between strain and stress can be read off from this diagram.
Clearly recognisable is that, at the beginning, there is a *linear* relationship between strain and stress.
A doubling of the strain therefore produces a stress twice as large.

![Stress-strain diagram of a mild steel](images/ArbeitsdiagrammStahl.svg){#fig-arbeitsdiagramm}

::: {.callout-important .plot-box icon=false}

The slope of the straight line is determined by the *modulus of elasticity* (Young's modulus).
This is a material parameter with the unit of a stress.
Up to the so-called *yield limit* $f_y$, there is a *linear* relationship between strain and stress of the form

$$
\myBox{\sigma = E\ve} \; .
$$ {#eq-hooke}

The above relation is also often called [Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law.
It holds in the so-called *elastic* range, i.e. when the stress is smaller than the yield limit, and only *here*!
Elastic material behaviour describes that when the force $F$ is reduced back to zero, the specimen returns to its *undeformed* initial state.
At the end the strain is therefore zero again.

If the yield limit is reached or exceeded, *plastic* material behaviour occurs.
First, the strain increases at constant stress.
Subsequently the stress can be increased again until necking of the specimen occurs, which in turn leads to fracture.
If the specimen experiences a load in the plastic range, i.e. $\sigma\geq f_y$, then upon complete unloading it does *not* return to the undeformed initial state!
A residual strain therefore remains in the specimen.

Within this lecture we consider only the initial, linear elastic range.
We therefore presuppose the validity of [Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law ([-@eq-hooke]).
Thus we have found a *linear* relationship between strain and stress, where the proportionality factor is the $E$-modulus (modulus of elasticity).
[Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law is applicable to many materials when restricted to small strains (displacements).
In @tbl-material the $E$-modulus is listed for common metallic and non-metallic materials.

| Material        | $E$ (N/mm²)                   | $\alpha$ (1/°C)                      |
|:----------------|:-----------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| Steel           | $2.1\cdot 10^5$               | $1.2\cdot 10^{-5}$                   |
| Aluminium       | $0.7\cdot 10^5$               | $2.3\cdot 10^{-5}$                   |
| Brass           | $1.0\cdot 10^5$               | $1.8\cdot 10^{-5}$                   |
| Cast iron       | $1.0\cdot 10^5$               | $0.9\cdot 10^{-5}$                   |
| Wood (in grain) | $0.7\ldots 2.0\cdot 10^4$     | $2.2\ldots 3.1\cdot 10^{-5}$         |
| Concrete        | $0.3\cdot 10^5$               | $1.0\cdot 10^{-5}$                   |
| Glass fibre     | $0.8\cdot 10^5$               |                                      |

: Material properties {#tbl-material}

Besides an external load, a *change* in temperature can also cause a strain (change in length).
If the bar is installed at a temperature $T_0$ and subsequently experiences a uniform^[*Every* point experiences the *same* change in temperature!] temperature change of $\Delta T$, then it can be shown experimentally that the strain is equal to

$$
\ve_T = \alpha\Delta T
$$ {#eq-dehnung-T}

The *coefficient of thermal expansion* $\alpha$ is another material parameter and is given in 1/°C, see @tbl-material.
Note that heating ($\Delta T>0$, $\Delta l>0$) leads to an elongation ($\ve_T>0$), and cooling ($\Delta T<0$) to a shortening ($\ve_T<0$, $\Delta l<0$).
Together with [Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law ([-@eq-hooke]), the strain due to external load and temperature change becomes

$$
\ve = \dfrac{\sigma}{E} + \alpha\Delta T \; .
$$ {#eq-dehnung-gesamt}

This relation can also be rewritten as

$$
\sigma = E(\ve-\alpha \Delta T) \; .
$$ {#eq-sigma-T}

::: {#exm-thermisch}
A bar of length $l$ and constant cross-section $A$ experiences a uniform temperature change $\Delta T$.
What differences arise for the two different supports of the bar?

![](images/thermischeDehnungBsp.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

Cutting the supports free:

![](images/thermischeDehnungBsp1.svg){fig-align="center"}

Statically determinate?

$$
\begin{align*}
\text{no!} & & \text{yes!}
\end{align*}
$$

Equilibrium condition in the horizontal direction $\sum H = 0$:

$$
\begin{align*}
\Cline[myBlue]{N(x)\neq 0} \rightarrow \sigma(x)\neq 0 & & N(x) = 0 \rightarrow \sigma(x) = 0
\end{align*}
$$

Longitudinal displacement $u$:

$$
\begin{align*}
u(x) = 0 \rightarrow \ve = 0 & & \Cline[myBlue]{u(x) \neq 0} \rightarrow \ve\neq0
\end{align*}
$$

From ([-@eq-sigma-T]) it thus follows:

$$
\begin{align*}
\ve = 0 = \dfrac{\sigma}{E} + \alpha\Delta T & & \ve = \dfrac{du}{dx} = \alpha\Delta T
\end{align*}
$$

Solving for the unknowns:

$$
\begin{align*}
\sigma(x) = -E\alpha\Delta T \rightarrow \Cline[myBlue]{N(x) = -EA\alpha\Delta T} & & du = \alpha\Delta T\, dx \rightarrow \int \rightarrow \Cline[myBlue]{u(x) = \alpha\Delta T x}
\end{align*}
$$

Interpret the solutions! What is the difference between $\Delta T>0$ and $\Delta T<0$?
:::

From this simple example we observe the following: in statically determinate systems a pure temperature change leads to strains (deformations) but to no stresses!
The situation is different for statically *in*determinate systems.
There, stresses and in general also deformations arise under a temperature change!

## Differential Equation for the Tension and Compression Bar {#sec-dgl-stab}

With the relations obtained, we now derive the governing equation (differential equation) of the tension or compression bar in @fig-allg-zugstab.

![General tension or compression bar](images/allgemeinerZugstab.svg){#fig-allg-zugstab}

This describes the mechanical behaviour of the bar under the action of a single force $F$ or a distributed longitudinal load $q$.

In mechanics, three categories of equations (relations) can be stated.
For the bar in @fig-allg-zugstab these are:

- **Equilibrium**

  $$
  \myfrac{dN}{dx} = -q(x)
  $$ {#eq-gg-stab}

  In words: the change of the normal force $N$ in the longitudinal direction $x$ of the bar is equal to the negative longitudinal load $q$!

- **Kinematic relations** (strain)

  $$
  \ve = \dfrac{du}{dx}
  $$ {#eq-kinematik}

- **Constitutive relations** (material law)

  $$
  \sigma = E\ve
  $$ {#eq-werkstoff}

From the kinematic and constitutive relations, taking into account ([-@eq-spannung]), the normal force follows as

$$
N = A\sigma = A\,E\ve = EA \dfrac{du}{dx} \; .
$$ {#eq-normalkraft}

Inserting into the equilibrium condition ([-@eq-gg-stab]) yields

$$
\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(EA\dfrac{du}{dx}\right) = -q(x) \; .
$$ {#eq-dgl-allg}

If it is assumed that the cross-section and the $E$-modulus do not change along the bar ($EA=$ const.), we finally obtain^[The two notations for the derivatives are identical: $\dfrac{d^2 u}{dx^2}\equiv u''$]

$$
\myBox{\dfrac{d^2u}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{q(x)}{EA}} \; .
$$ {#eq-dgl}

This *linear* differential equation describes the mechanical behaviour of the tension or compression bar.
By solving ([-@eq-dgl]) we can, for a known external load, determine the longitudinal displacement $u$, and subsequently, with the kinematic and constitutive relations, the strain and stress.

::: {#exm-haengender-stab}
Determine the displacement and stress distribution of a hanging bar under self-weight and a single load!

![](images/haengenderStab.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

The self-weight of the bar per unit length is given by

$$
q(x)\equiv q_0 = \rho A g \; .
$$

The differential equation ([-@eq-dgl]) therefore reads

$$
\dfrac{d^2u}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{q_0}{EA} \; .
$$

By separation of the variables,

$$
d^2u = -\dfrac{q_0}{EA}\,dx^2 \; ,
$$

and subsequent double integration we obtain:

$$
u(x) = -\dfrac{q_0}{EA}\dfrac{x^2}{2} + C_1x + C_2 \; .
$$ {#eq-bsp-u}

Now the constants of integration still have to be adapted to the *boundary conditions*.
At the upper end of the bar the following must hold:

$$
u(x=0) = 0 \; .
$$

From this it follows immediately that $C_2=0$.
At the lower end we cannot make any statement about the displacement, but we can about the stress:

$$
\sigma(x=l) = \dfrac{F}{A} \; .
$$

But how is the stress computed?
Via [Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law ([-@eq-hooke]) and the strain ([-@eq-dehnung-dudx]) as

$$
\sigma = E\ve = E\dfrac{du}{dx} \; .
$$

Inserting the longitudinal displacement ([-@eq-bsp-u]) and evaluating at the position $x=l$ gives:

$$
\sigma(x=l)=E\ve\big|_{x=l} = E\dfrac{du}{dx}\Bigg|_{x=l} = E\left(-\dfrac{q_0x}{EA}+C_1\right)\Bigg|_{x=l} = E\left(-\dfrac{q_0l}{EA}+C_1\right)=\dfrac{F}{A} \; ,
$$

from which $C_1$ can be determined as

$$
C_1 = \dfrac{1}{EA}\left(F+q_0l\right) \; .
$$

Thus the displacement along the bar is given by

$$
u(x) = \dfrac{1}{EA}\left(-\dfrac{q_0x^2}{2}+q_0lx+Fx\right) \; .
$$

Sketch this distribution and the associated stress distribution!
:::

Using the above example we want to emphasise the important significance of a linear mechanical system.
The external load on the hanging bar can be divided into two *load cases* (LC):

$$
\color{myBlue}{\text{LC 1}}\rightarrow q_0 \quad \text{and} \quad \color{myOrange}{\text{LC 2}}\rightarrow F \; .
$$

Because of the *linear* behaviour, and the resulting *linear* differential equation ([-@eq-dgl]), we can compute each LC *separately* and subsequently *add* (or superpose) the results.
This possibility of computation is called the *principle of superposition*.
For example, the total displacement is then composed of the sum of the individual LCs:

$$
u(x) = u_{LF\;1} + u_{LF\;2} + u_{LF\;3} + \ldots \; .
$$ {#eq-superposition}

This can also be seen in the result of the previous example:

$$
u(x) = u_{\color{myBlue}{LF\;1}} \bs{+} u_{\color{myOrange}{LF\;2}} = \dfrac{1}{EA}\left(\Cline[myBlue]{\color{myBlue}{q_0}(x^2-lx)} \bs{+} \Cline[myOrange]{\color{myOrange}{F}x}\right) \, .
$$ {#eq-superposition-bsp}

The same applies to every other mechanical quantity, as in this case stress and strain.

If at least one of the fundamental relations (equilibrium, kinematic and constitutive relations) has a nonlinear character, then the mechanical behaviour is no longer linear!
As an example, [Hooke]{.smallcaps}'s law is replaced by a nonlinear elastic material law of the form

$$
\sigma = C\ln(1+\ve)
$$ {#eq-gummi}

where $C$ is a material parameter to be determined experimentally. Rubber exhibits such behaviour.
In @fig-gummi the associated stress-strain diagram is shown.

![Nonlinear elastic material behaviour](images/MaterialGummi.svg){#fig-gummi}

The mechanical behaviour is then determined by the *nonlinear* differential equation^[cf. the *linear* differential equation ([-@eq-dgl])!]

$$
CA\,\color{myBlue}{\dfrac{1}{1+\dfrac{du}{dx}}}\,\dfrac{d^2u}{dx^2} = q(x) \; .
$$ {#eq-dgl-nichtlinear}

In this case the principle of superposition is *no longer* valid and applicable!
A decisive disadvantage in practical computation.

## Simply Statically Indeterminate Systems {#sec-statisch-unbestimmt}

For statically indeterminate systems the equilibrium conditions are not sufficient to determine the support reactions and the internal bar forces.
With the help of so-called *kinematic constraint conditions* one obtains additional equations for the computation of such systems.
We discuss the procedure by means of an example.
Beforehand, the essential steps can be stated as follows:

- Releasing a constraint – reduction to a statically *determinate* system.
- Computation of the displacement/deformation that arises at the location and in the direction of the released constraint, on the statically determinate system due to the external load.
- Applying the force $X$, unknown in magnitude, associated with the released constraint on the statically determinate system and determining the displacement/deformation at the location and in the direction of $X$.
- Setting up a kinematic constraint condition and computing the force $X$ from it.

::: {#exm-starre-platte}
A *rigid*, weightless plate is suspended from three bars.
Rigid means that it does not deform! Two bars have an axial stiffness of $EA_1$, the third one of magnitude $EA_2$.
All bars have the same length $l$. Bar $1$ experiences a temperature change of magnitude $\Delta T$.
At point $A$ the rigid plate is held horizontally.
The normal forces in the three bars are to be computed!

![](images/abgehaengterStab.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

To make the sought bar forces visible, we cut the rigid plate out, severing bars $1$ to $3$, and then enter all forces^[Enter normal forces as positive in tension!] in a sketch (method of sections):

![](images/abgehaengterStab2.svg){fig-align="center"}

Four unknown forces appear in the cut.
For a planar force system, however, only three equilibrium conditions are available.
Consequently, this is a *simply* ($4-3=1$) statically *indeterminate* system.
The three equilibrium conditions read:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum H=0: &\quad A_H = 0 \\
\sum V=0: &\quad N_1 + N_2 + N_3 = 0 \\
\sum M^{(A)} = 0: &\quad N_1\dfrac{a}{2} + N_2\dfrac{3a}{2} + N_3\dfrac{5a}{2} = 0 \;.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-gg-platte}

From the first it follows immediately that $A_H=0$.
From the remaining two, however, we cannot compute the three unknown normal forces.

In order to be able to compute the normal forces nonetheless, we proceed as follows.
Now a constraint is released.
In the present case this means that bar $3$ is severed immediately above its connection to the rigid plate.
This renders the bar ineffective, i.e. the normal force in the bar is zero ($N_3=0$).
Through this step a statically *determinate* system is obtained.
Consequently, the normal forces $N_1$ and $N_2$ as well as $A_H$ can be determined from the equilibrium conditions ([-@eq-gg-platte]).

![](images/abgehaengterStab3.svg){fig-align="center"}

Which constraint of the statically indeterminate system is released is immaterial.
Bar $1$ or bar $3$ can also be severed.

If now bar $1$ in the above system experiences a temperature change of $\Delta T$, the normal forces $1$ and $2$ are equal to zero!^[Why, actually? Consider the equilibrium!]
Consequently, the normal stress is also zero, and from ([-@eq-dehnung-gesamt]) one obtains for the strain in bar $1$

$$
\ve = \alpha\Delta T \; .
$$

This is *constant* over the length of the bar, and according to ([-@eq-dehnung]) the change in length due to the temperature change (superscript $T$) is then^[Note: if heating occurs ($\Delta T>0$), then bar $1$ experiences an elongation ($\Delta l_1^{(T)}>0$). Upon cooling ($\Delta T<0$) the bar is shortened ($\Delta l_1^{(T)}<0$).]:

$$
\Delta l_1^{(T)} = \ve l = \alpha\Delta T l \; .
$$

At the location where bar $3$ was severed, we obtain an overlap of the two bar ends of magnitude

$$
\Delta l_3^{(T)} = - \Delta l_1^{(T)} \; .
$$

This overlap naturally does not occur in the real system!
In bar $2$ neither a normal force nor a temperature change acts.
It therefore experiences no strain and its length thus remains unchanged.
This results in the plate displacement under temperature action shown above.

Now a force $X$, unknown in magnitude, is applied at the two ends of the severed bar.
This corresponds to the normal force in bar $3$.
Since, in the real system, a compressive force acts in bar $3$ due to a positive temperature change, we also apply $X$ in this way.

![](images/abgehaengterStab4.svg){fig-align="center"}

By cutting free and via the equilibrium conditions one obtains the normal forces, constant over the length, in bars $1$ and $2$ due to $X$:

$$
N_1^{(X)} = -X \quad \text{and} \quad N_2^{(X)} = 2X\; .
$$

In the upper sketch these are entered with correct signs. Knowing the normal force, we can again determine the respective change in length of the bars using ([-@eq-dehnung]) and ([-@eq-dehnung-gesamt]):

$$
\Delta l_1^{(X)}= \ve l = \dfrac{\sigma}{E}l = \dfrac{N_1^{(X)}}{EA_1}l = -\dfrac{Xl}{EA_1}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\Delta l_2^{(X)}= \dfrac{N_2^{(X)}}{EA}l = \dfrac{2Xl}{EA_1} \; .
$$

From geometric considerations (equation of a straight line), a gap of the severed bar ends of bar $3$ results for this load case as:

$$
\Delta l_3^{(X)}=\Delta l_1^{(X)} +\dfrac{\Delta l_2^{(X)}-\Delta l_1^{(X)}}{a}2a = 2\Delta l_2^{(X)}-\Delta l_1^{(X)} = \dfrac{5Xl}{EA_1} \; .
$$

This depends on the magnitude of $X$.

![](images/abgehaengterStab5.svg){fig-align="center"}

In the following sketch the vertical displacement of the lower severed bar end (blue line) due to temperature change and force $X$ is shown.
The unknown force $X$ also acts, however, on the upper part of the hanging bar $3$.
The vertical displacement of the upper bar end (orange line) is

$$
\Delta l_3 = -\dfrac{Xl}{EA_2} \; .
$$

But how large are the vertical displacements of the two severed bar ends in the real system?

![](images/abgehaengterStab6.svg){fig-align="center"}

These *must* be at the same position, i.e. there must be neither a gap nor an overlap at the severed location!
From this we can set up the following kinematic compatibility

$$
\Delta l_3^{(T)} + \Delta l_3^{(X)} = \Delta l_3 \; .
$$

And from this we can determine the unknown force $X$:

$$
X = \dfrac{1}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\,EA_1\alpha\Delta T \; .
$$

Since $X$ was applied as a compressive force on bar $3$, $N_3=-X$. By solving the equilibrium conditions ([-@eq-gg-platte]) we then obtain the two other normal forces:

$$
N_1 = -\dfrac{1}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\,EA_1\alpha\Delta T \qquad
N_2 = \dfrac{2}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\,EA_1\alpha\Delta T \; .
$$

Knowing the normal forces, the change in length of the bars can subsequently be determined:

$$
\Delta l_1= \left(1-\dfrac{1}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\right)\alpha\Delta T l \qquad
\Delta l_2= \dfrac{2}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\alpha\Delta T l \qquad
\Delta l_3= -\dfrac{1}{5+\dfrac{EA_1}{EA_2}}\alpha\Delta T l \; .
$$

In @fig-steifigkeitsverhaeltnis the normal force in the bars and their change in length are shown for different stiffness ratios $EA_1/EA_2$.
This clearly shows that for a statically *indeterminate* system the support reactions and internal forces also depend on the stiffness ratio!

The marked points represent the solution for the axially rigid bar, i.e. $EA_2\rightarrow\infty$.
In this case the change in length of bar $3$ is equal to zero.
The other limiting case, $EA_2=0$, is equivalent to the absence of the bar.
Then the system would be statically determinate.

From these results important conclusions can be drawn:

- In statically *determinate* systems ($EA_2=0$), a temperature change causes deformations, but *no* additional forces!
- If the system is statically *indeterminate*, a temperature change leads to deformations *and* additional forces!

![Normal forces and changes in length of the bars as a function of the stiffness ratio $EA_1/EA_2$](images/axialForceRatio.svg){#fig-steifigkeitsverhaeltnis}
:::

::: {#exm-vordach}
Given is the structural system of a canopy. Both bars have the same axial stiffness $EA$.
Compute the bar forces, their change in length, and the horizontal and vertical displacement of point $A$! *Small* displacements are assumed!

![](images/Vordach.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

- Bar forces: $S_1 = \dfrac{2F}{\sqrt{3}}, \; S_2=-\dfrac{F}{\sqrt{3}}$
- Change in length: $\Delta l_1 = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{Fl}{EA}, \; \Delta l_2 = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{Fl}{EA}$
- Horizontal and vertical displacement: $u_H = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{Fl}{EA},\; u_V = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\Delta l_1 + \sqrt{3}|\Delta l_2| = 3\dfrac{Fl}{EA}$
:::

::: {#exm-drei-staebe}
Determine the normal forces in bars $1$ to $3$ as well as the horizontal and vertical displacement of point $A$!

![](images/DreiStabe.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

- Bar forces: $S_1 = \dfrac{F}{3}\;, \; S_2 = -F\;, \; S_3 =-\dfrac{2F}{3}$
- Horizontal and vertical displacement: $u_H=\dfrac{Fl}{3EA}\;, \; u_V=\dfrac{Fl}{EA}$
:::

::: {#exm-starre-platte-T}
A rigid plate is loaded by a single force $F$ and held by two bars.
How large is the deflection at point $A$?
By how much would bar $1$ have to be heated so that no deflection occurs?

![](images/starrePlatteT.svg){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

- Bar forces: $S_1 = -2F,\;S_2 = -F$
- Deflection: $u_V = \dfrac{3Fl}{EA}$
- Heating: $\Delta T = +\dfrac{3F}{2\alpha EA}$
:::

::: {#exm-seilbagger}
We consider a simplified model of a cable excavator.
The boom and the back-anchoring are treated as bars with an axial stiffness of $42000\,\text{kN/cm}$.
At the common point $A$ of the two bars a deflection pulley with a radius of $30\,\text{cm}$ is mounted.
The cable with a length of $15\,\text{m}$ and an axial stiffness of $21000\,\text{kN/cm}$ is guided frictionlessly from the suspension point $B$ around this pulley to the winch.
At point $B$ a mass of $2000\,\text{kg}$ is attached to the cable.

![](images/Winde.svg){fig-align="center"}

For the static case, the following are sought:

1) Cable force before and after the deflection pulley.
2) Force action on bars $1$ and $2$ at point $A$.
3) Computation of the normal force in bar $1$ and bar $2$.
4) Horizontal and vertical displacement of point $A$.
5) By how much does point $B$ lower in total?
:::

::: {.callout-tip .loesung collapse="true" icon=false}
## Solution

1) $S_\text{vor}=S_\text{nach}=19.62\,\text{kN}$
2) $F_H=17.0\,\text{kN} \quad F_V=29.43\,\text{kN}$
3) $S_1=33.99\,\text{kN} \quad S_2=0$
4) $u_H=0.19\,\text{cm} \quad u_V=0.32\,\text{cm}$
5) $u_V=1.72\,\text{cm}$
:::
